content:
I formalized @Harald Helfgott proof of the Ternary Goldbach at https://github.com/gersh/ternary-goldbach-lean. This is the proof every odd number greater than 7 is the sum of three primes.

The proof involves extensive finite computations. Where native_decide wasn't feasible, code in other languages is referenced in the repo, and was run to verify except for a few very computationally intensive parts, which are left as citations, and axiomatized. All analytic parts of the proof were formalized in Lean.

This required many theorems from analytics number theory with tight bounds, which weren't already in mathlib. So, I had the AI build them.

I tried to build re-usable components for various aspects of the proof, which are in the ext directory.
I haven't read the code yet but it is interesting there is something even native_decide can't handle
This formalization is full of axioms.

Thank you for the feedback. The axioms are all finite computations with citations, and scripts to compute them. A few are super computationally intensive, but I'm going try converting the rest to native_decide.

This sounds like exciting news; congratulations. At the same time, I would like to understand several aspects of this claimed formalization more precisely.

a) Which version of the proof is it based on?

There are several public versions: the original papers, the 2015 book draft, and the revised chapters released from 2019 onward; there are also newer chapters that are not yet public.

The repository suggests that the formalization is a hybrid: mainly arXiv:1501.05438v2, sometimes using the numbering of arXiv:1312.7748v2, together with the v4 major- and minor-arc papers, but that the revised chapters were not used. Is that accurate?

A dependency map indicating the source used for each major part would be very helpful.

b) The early versions naturally contain some local errors. (I have talked with colleagues, editors, and more particularly people in the formal-proof community about them.) They are neither fatal nor particularly serious - in fact they are more annoying than anything else - but a formalization cannot ignore them.

Part of the point of the 2019 revision was to avoid feasible but awkward local repairs (henceforth: "masking tape") by taking cleaner routes.

I would be very interested in a systematic account of what was done. I suspect that, if everything typechecks, then either AI or humans recurred to masking tape. That's perfectly legitimate, and it is not astounding if that is within AI's autonomous capabilities by now. It also confirms what I've implied, namely, that this was very doable without new ideas - it is just not how I personally prefer to do things, at least when writing for human beings.

Don't take it negatively - if anything, it takes a bit of pressure off from me; somewhere, someone must have been unhappy that I have to been taken the longer route for the sake of what they may have seen as 'just' elegance, and they are presumably happy now, or may soon be. I would, however, like to know how much help and handholding the AI needed, if any, both on this matter as in many others.

c) What exactly is the trust boundary?

The repository reports that the dependency cone of the final theorem has no "sorry"s. It contains 4,659 generated native_decide atoms and 22 named external/source atoms, all described as bounded computations, finite tables or verified-zero inputs. Is this really correct?

There seem to be three possibilities:

c1) that these are really bounded computations and finite tables. That is fair enough - some computations are both massive and carried out very rigorously; formalizing them would be a different project, probably to be carried outside Lean - by means of fast code that is verified to be correct, for instance.

c2) that these are results in the literature. Then the situation is not wholly satisfactory, though in the same way that any result that relies on the still formally-unverified explicit ANT literature (including essentially all work in explicit number theory, my own work up to very recently not excepted) is not wholly satisfactory, in my view. See (d).

c3) that these are parts of the proof itself that are taken on trust. Then what we have at hand would not be really a formalization, but the beginning of one.

A quick reading suggests this text is mostly at (c2). There are also elements of (c1), which, as I said, is satisfactory and most likely unavoidable right now - but I'm not sure they are carried out satisfactorily; there seems to be a certificate for a claim up to 10^16 that is only actually run up to 550000, for instance. If that claim is actually supported in the literature, then that's fine (or (c2) at worst), but it would be good to go over things point by point.

I would, however, want to be able to rule out that we are at (c3).

d) More on (c2), or rather a closely related matter.

I am still working on a definitive version of the proof. The main reason (other than my being busy with other projects) is analogous to how some people stop eating sausage after visiting the sausage factory.

To wit: earlier versions of my proof (including the chapters made public in 2019) relied on standard explicit results in the literature. Unfortunately, some of them, while in all likelihood correct, have proofs that leave something to be desired (e.g., one refers to a paper that only exists as an extended abstract - and many rely on papers that rely on papers than rely on other papers, often with non-fatal slips in the proofs). Note also that some papers on arxiv are quite simply incorrect.

What I decided to do a couple of years back was to make to reconstruct a substantial part of the basic estimates in explicit analytic number theory from scratch. See my preprints, joint with Andrés Chirre:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14736
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.15709
The repository already uses the second paper. A human-led team has been formalizing this material and is not far from completing important parts of it.
This is part of a broader effort to formalize explicit analytic number theory:

https://www.ipam.ucla.edu/news-research/special-projects/integrated-explicit-analytic-number-theory-network/

We should discuss how these projects relate, how their dependency boundaries compare, and how reusable work can be shared rather than duplicated.

e) I am helping with formalizing (d). In the process, there have been some obstacles, due to basic analytic tools that were not available in Mathlib.

For instance: something that one needs quite often in analytic number theory and in Fourier analysis is to integrate by parts when one function is C^1 and the other is of bounded variation. This is not wholly without the abilities of AI, and in fact I managed to formalize much of what was needed in January using an AI, but it was rather painful and certainly not automatic; the resulting code was also ugly.

However, it was a useful proof-of-concept, in that it showed conclusively that Appendix A in Montgomery-Vaughan could serve as a template for formalization. Then a team of people in May (including several young people, Terry Tao and theoretically me, but I was mostly just impressed at how fluently young people code in Lean, and indicated what I had done in January) produced some human-generated code fulfilling the task completely.

I wonder what this formalization has done about this matter; has it dealt with it, can it really be avoided completely, or does it assume standard results that rely on it? Mind you, this is only one of several basic analytic issues that one has to resolve in order to formalize analytic number theory, particularly explicit results. I do know AI was already able to help greatly earlier this year - I spent some of January and February feeding Aristotle chunks of Wheeden-Zygmund; after many Heimlich maneuvers, it managed to formalize them in ways that mostly type-checked. Still, it's an issue that cannot be avoided, and, if it was successfully dealt with, it would be good to know how.

a) It is a combination of papers. I gave it every paper I could find, and then had it basically do whatever worked. Whenever it got stuck with something, I'd try to find a paper with a solution. Initially, I was very loose at following any paper. It would claim there were only a "few residuals" left, before finding counterexample in half of them, and needing to figure out how to salvage things. Although, then the AI would get overconfident with "shortcuts," which often didn't pan out, and so I told it be paper-faithful, and it would just follow whatever paper was needed was needed to deal with residuals. Although, it was able to invent its own stuff where needed too.

I put together a dependency map.

b) I detected the errors in papers when I while doing the proof. I had the AI put together a list of paper errors, and how they were corrected. I tried to get to determine how it was corrected, but I can't guarantee that is 100% accurate.

The AI would used sympy extensively, and it was constantly testing and finding errors. A lot of it was transcription errors, and I tried get it to distinguish what was in the paper. Initially, it just kept adding axioms to get around problems, but many of the axioms weren't even true. Later, I started forbidding it from adding axioms, but then it would add conditional theorems (I.E. instead of proving A --> B, it would prove A \and X --> B), where X is some question able axiom. A lot of effort went into getting to stop doing this, and figuring out how to get it to behave. I focused on telling model to be paper-faithful. After the first month of working on this, I had it start writing songs every-day. If you want to get a sense of how the AI approached things, you can look at the songs.

c) The current trust boundary is documented in the Citations Directory along with existing native decides. They are all computations. I was also able to replicate most of them with my own code in Python or C, which is included in the repo. The Chirre-Helfgott

I realized I can actually convert more stuff to native decide, and I have an AI chugging away at it right now. I think I should be able to convert most everything to native decide.

d) I dealt extensively with formalizing basic analytic number theory results. I fed the AI multiple analytics number theory textbooks, and also tracked down the original papers where needed. Basically, I had look for all dependencies that weren't in mathlib, and then had it figure out what source they were in, figured out how to obtain the source, and then had the AI formalize everything. The AI had would complain it was impossible or difficult when major things weren't in mathlib, but then I imbued with do it yourself spirit, it started using a ":working_on_it:" emoji in everything, and embraced the DIY spirit.

It took a while, but eventually it had built up all the basic analytic number theory infrastructure to start building on. After it built the infrastructure, there some challenges in getting it to keep tracking of its own infrastructure, and use its own infrastructure. The model was trained with the world as mathlib was, and then I had make sure it was prompted to know it now had powerful new infrastructure for proving stuff.

I didn't really bother to verify whether it faithfully proved the theorems because I was just trying to ternary Goldbach. So, if there were in transcription or whatever, I'd just wait for it show up in the trust surface as problems in the capstone proof, or at least a high-leve lemma.

I do depend on some results from Chirre-Helfgott papers, so if those are formalized that would be complete the formalization.

(e) I'm not sure if I have the specific theorem you are referring to, but there is substantial infrastructure around fourier analysis and integration by parts. Seeext/analytic_nt/AnalyticNT/Diophantine/FourierIntegrableC2CompactSupport.lean in the AnalyticNT module. There is also in MathExtras https://github.com/gersh/ternary-goldbach-lean/blob/d6de6f92a856a804a5abf8e33465356a86a0bbaa/MathExtras/Analysis/Fourier/QuantitativeIBP.lean.

Many classic analytic number theorem results are hiding in the repo, often base trio. I also built infrastructure for proving tight bounds on things through various methods if you look at ext modules--some even have examples and proof strategies.

I think it'd be cool to have to just build out stronger infrastructure, where you just give all sorts functions, and then it can just prove various bounds on it. Effective Asymptotics under ext started doing some of that, but I haven't actually tried playing with it manually. I had the AI build a bunch of stuff that could probably become its own modules for proving analytic number theory bounds and such.

@Gershon Bialer if you want a serious review of your I suggest the following:

  • first of all add comparator. It will say that you use axioms, but at least we can check the statement.
  • put all the axioms in one single lean file, adding to each one a precise reference in the literature (and a LaTeX statement).
  • avoid as much as possible software engineer terminology like " There is exactly one comparison card per live atom; inventory.json is the machine-readable one-to-one map." is you want mathematicians to be involved. We are simply not used to this terminology and I just think it doesn't work for a math work.
  • concerning native_decide I am less sure, but I would be more interested in avoiding it completely, even if the cost is adding more axioms.

Then the real question is: "how many axioms are still there?" Can the author, i.e. @Harald Helfgott, say something about those? For example if Harald say "I am sure this is correct, it's a well known theorem" it's a thing, if they say "this is the main subtle point" it is something very different.

I honestly think that the repo in the current status is extremely difficult to review.

(a) So you didn't use the 2019 material on my webpage at all? (c) Do you actually mean the AI has given certified proofs of the results in the literature my work uses? (e) Integration by parts when both functions are C^1 is one thing - of course that's in mathlib. But something as basic as integration by parts when one function is C^1 and one function in BV isn't in mathlib yet. (That's basic in many senses .) Proving that requires work in foundations, and, while that's wholly standard for a human mathematician, from my experience earlier this year, AI finds it remarkably difficult.

Riccardo Brasca schrieb:

concerning native_decide I am less sure, but I would be more interested in avoiding it completely, even if the cost is adding more axioms.

In case you didn't know, the effect of native_decide is to create an axiom.

I what what it does. What I am less sure is if it's better to trust native_decide, so the whole compiler, or a a mathematical result that I find in the literature (or even a computation made with sage or whatever)
Right; I suppose in theory you could verify them individually but yeah there are probably too many to do that. It would probably make sense to at least reduce the amount of them.

This is why a single file with all of them would be useful. One can have an axiom file and also a file with everything that is proved by native_decide. Depending on the amount of stuff there we can think if it is worth to do something or not.

Harald Helfgott said:

I am still working on a definitive version of the proof.

Maybe this is off-topic for this Zulip, but do you have an estimate for when your definitive version will be finished? It's going to be a book, right?

Yes. The issue is that I have a bunch of other things to do, including some that have become urgent. One of those things is sending off for publication my papers with Chirre, though, and that feeds directly into the book.

You know what, let me ask ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to formalize something much more modest in scale - a four-page paper from 1985 that gets routinely used (often indirectly; that's how I used it, back in the day) and that I now know to be both flawed (and not just because it is essentially an extended abstract) and fixable. (In fact, I had a master's student fix it for his thesis last year.) Perhaps people with better subscriptions can do the same with Fable and then we can compare. This may already be worthwhile, mainly as a reality check. It involves mainly elementary arguments, and so it doesn't involve the thorny basic analytic issues that I discussed above.

@Riccardo Brasca Thank you for the feedback. I will look into adding comparator. Admittedly, this is actually kinda my first proof in Lean, and so I haven't really been familiar with conventions on stuff. I just asked the AI what to do on everything. I will look into how to make it more readable.

I think properly comparing the equations in papers with the lean axioms may be one of the more challenging things. I will look more into how to do this better. It seems like the AI seemed to have an annoying habit splitting the equations from theorems, making it harder to tell theorem is actually proving sometimes.

I use thousands of native_decides. A lot of them are just numeric inequalities of basic functions, where it is just trying to prove it is less than some fraction. I suppose verification would be a matter of making sure it isn't doing some weird floating arithmetic that is messing up the calculations. They probably could all be properly formalized with proper interval arithmetic if it is worth it.

@Harald Helfgott I used Codex and Claude Code. I had the most success with Codex using it in ultra mode. I think Fable is the best at finding errors in papers, but it can eat tokens super-fast, and then may look almost done before it demands additional payment.

I do sorta recall it going how it figured out how to use proof by contradiction coerce things into different forms for integration by parts proofs, but I don't know exactly what it did.

I have other things to do myself right now, but I should have more time later to work on this.

"(a) So you didn't use the 2019 material on my webpage at all?"
I gave the AI the 2019 material. I'm not entirely sure how much it used it. I had multiple routes in the repo, and then it was putting things together, and then I tried it prune it later, and it seemed like it struggled to complete the 2019 route, but I think it probably used at least some of the ideas from it.
"c) Do you actually mean the AI has given certified proofs of the results in the literature my work uses?"
Essentially yes. It may have figured it could use weaker versions, or found a workaround for some things. Things that don't depend on heavy computation were generally proven base trio.

This didn't just happen. I used the memory and skills features of codex and claude code along with figuring out how to prompt it. It did get stuck quite a bit, and I had to figure out how to get it unstuck. I started at the beginning of May, and the models have improved substantially since then, which definitely helped.

I proved a lot classical stuff base trio, which would probably be significant formalizations in their own right. I made a doc showing what I proved base trio . This includes stuff like Σn≥1 μ(n)/n² = 6/π², which unlocked various things.

(What do you mean by 'base trio'?)

So, what did you do about results in the literature of the form ∣M(x)∣≤ϵx|M(x)|\leq \epsilon x∣M(x)∣≤ϵx, ∣M(x)∣≤cx/log⁡x|M(x)|\leq c x/\log x∣M(x)∣≤cx/logx, $$m(x)\leq c/\log x$? Are you quoting them, or proving them?

By base trio, I just mean Lean's three foundational axioms.

I prove for x >= 2160535 |M(x)| <= x/4345. This depends on:
finite computations from
H. Cohen, F. Dress, and M. El Marraki, *Explicit estimates
for summatory functions linked to the Moebius mu-function*, Functiones et
Approximatio 37.1 (2007), 51--63, which my Python code also verified. It looks like I can probably also turn this into a native_decide.
Hurst 2018 (see https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.08551v2) is relied on for finite computation

For the finite range |M(x)| < \epsilon*sqrt(x) over a finite range, I again use Hurst. The same sqrt bound is used to prove the linear bound above.

I prove for y>=2 m(y) <= .347/log(y). It depends on the Chirre-Helfgott computations, the previous big Merten cites, the Ramare Martens 2025 paper, and the little Mertens finite bound up to 7,727,068,587 from the 2012 Minor Arcs Paper. Although, I replicate the Ramare Martens cite with my own Python. Others papers like Rosser-Schoenfeld and parts of Chirre-Helfgott are formalized with finite decides.

The essential finite computations not replicated are: Chirre-Helfgott Chapter 25 lemma A.7 and lemma 9.2, and the little Mertens finite range computation.

@Gershon Bialer I am sorry but I really don't see the point of this work in its current status.

Numerical calculations are one of the main subtle points in the proof, and computer algebra system already made mistake in exactly those proofs, so dismissing them with native_decide or python is precisely dismissing one of the main points. And if there are thousands of places where this is done it's practically impossible to check whether we learnt something or not. Note also that I am more or less sure that native_decide contains bugs and one can prove False with it. By this I don't mean that it is badly implemented or whatever, but just that it is a big piece of software and so it's absolutely normal that it contains bugs. I also think that most likely a human being will not prove False by accident, but the point with LLM is that if their realize that there is a crazy bugs with Type 24235253454353 + 1 they will happely use it.

Concerning the mathematical proofs I repeat my point above, we need a clear file with the axioms that can be easily checked by a human being. I understand it's not easy, but well, this is a huge proof.

Having saying that let me stress that I don't think there is nothing valuable here, but currently it's basically impossible to judge and you cannot expect experts putting a lot of effort in studying it.

Riccardo Brasca said:

@Gershon Bialer I am sorry but I really don't see the point of this work in its current status.

It seems like in its current status, the point is to prove everything except a bunch of finite computations? That still seems useful to me?

That would be useful, but it doesn't seem the current status, for two reasons:

  • there are axioms, and we need to see what they say exactly (maybe are just computations, but that's my point, we need to see an easily readable file).
  • It's likely that native_decide is used only to perform computations, but I personally cannot trust this if it's used thousands of times.

Note that the full proof can be seen as a finite computation. The conjecture was already know starting from an explicit bound (I am not saying by any means that the work was only a bunch of computations of course).

It is suggested above that the axioms (both native_decide and otherwise) used correspond to specific finite computations that were involved (directly or indirectly) in Helfgott's proof.
Regarding the literal axioms (as opposed to native_decides): https://github.com/gersh/ternary-goldbach-lean/tree/main/problems/ternary-goldbach/citations is AI slop, but honestly not that bad to read as far as it goes.

Maybe there is a misunderstanding about the goal of such a project. In my opinion the goal is to convince people that the proof is correct.

Note that personally I already think it is correct because I trust the author. If course everyone can make mistakes, so it's reasonable to ask for a very high standard of certainty, like a formal proof. It seems to me that a formal proof as it's usually intended it's out of scope for this project, so now we have to decide if the work is more trustworthy than the human written proof. This may be subjective but it seems difficult to judge at the moment, for the reasons I explained above.

Really, I don't see why we cannot have a file with, say, 30 axioms, in Lean, and zero axioms in the rest of the project. I don't see the point of a bunch of md files: how can I be sure that this is the exact list of axioms used in the project?

I know it may seems paranoid, but on the other hand being sure of correctness seems the only goal. If there is some interesting mathematics/formalization then it's a different story, but it doesn't seem to be case.

Boris Alexeev said:

It is suggested above that the axioms (both native_decide and otherwise) used correspond to specific finite computations that were involved (directly or indirectly) in Helfgott's proof.

It is suggested... but how could I actually audit that? As far as I can tell, one would need to comb through a bunch of md files and make sure they actually correspond to computations in Helfgott's proof; Then read through a bunch of python scripts to check that they implement the computations correctly; And then also believe that none of the 1000+ native_decide's are doing anything bad.

The trust surface area to check here is a bit too large to be useful imo.

TL;DR: I suggest scaling back and starting at a smaller scale, with more basic results that are used in the Ternary Goldbach proof (or its publicly available versions).

I do think that formalization for the sake of correctness is particularly valuable in explicit analytic number theory. Most mathematicians are not particularly good at adding restaurant bills - and more complicated version of that are a necessary if uninteresting part of explicit work (in fact some seem to have the mistaken work that that's the main part of explicit work, or all of it; that's another matter).

At the same time, both for its own sake and to make sure that the check is correct, we want to have an easily readable text explaining what has been done - in particular, giving a human-readable version of whatever has been fixed or wasn't clear. I agree with others that a mathematician(s) + AI team is best here.

Yesterday, I talked with ChatGPT Sol about a 1985 paper that is a somewhat notorious weak link in the explicit literature - it appeared only as an extended abstract, and it is clear that intermediate steps contained errors, even if the results were correct. (I had already contacted the authors, who had also found there were issues, and who had ways to prove intermediate results that were sharper in some ways but neither stronger nor weaker, strictly speaking. I had also directed a master's thesis on the matter of fixing the paper).

At first, ChatGPT Sol didn't quite see the issue, and then suggested a computation that was much too large. However, with some prodding, it managed to find a rather clever way to fix the proof of the intermediate result, and reduced matters to a small computation that can presumably be carried out even in Lean.

Should I open a thread about this?
If you want some help with explicit computation yes! I think #**maths> is the appropriate streaming. And we have people that know how to do computation in Lean (without native_decide).

I think one important value of a project like this, which defers computations to native_decide or axiom backed up by literature citations, is to provoke others into discovering how we can do these computations properly in Lean. Lean certainly has limitations here, and some things that native_decide can unreliably answer will never be answerable in "pure" Lean, but that gap between where we are and the ceiling is enormous.

So again: a single entry point showing where native_decide is being used becomes a list of challenges for people interested in computation in Lean.

All of the computations can in theory be done in Lean kernel, but it may take a really long time to compile--perhaps, longer than my lifetime. Even if it just take hours to compile, it can make working with it very painful.

The second problem is just matter of your compute budget. Some of the verifications like Platt's Riemann-Zeta function zeros verifications used enormous compute resources. If you believe the Riemann Hypothesis, then I suppose it easy to trust verifications of it.

The calculations aren't necessarily very profound. It can just be a matter of proving the logarithm of something is less than some fraction.

(LeanCert tries to tackle some of this, but still doesn't fully get away from using native_decide. I'm working on a version the reduce number of native_decides, but I don't think it is feasible to run everything in kernel. I'm also working on refactoring to make it clearer what depends on native_decide, and including using LeanArchitect.

The truth is everyone is currently using native_decide for more difficult computations. I have some ideas on how to fix this, and I'm working on prototyping some of them.

I suspect few would demand a Lean recomputation of Platt's interval arithmetic-based certified zeta zeros computation. But small things that can be done in a "short time" eg Mathematica on a personal machine can be done once in a separate Lean file (like the PNT+ log tables) and referred to.
I updated the repo, and added a blueprint-generated doc.

Some brief words (I'm leading a summer school under an active volcano and have a negative amount of time): I played with ChatGPT 5.6 during the weekend, and yes: (a) it can find all errors (largely typos and contained local errors) known to me in the (January 2015 version), and some unknown to me, though, fortunately, they are few and local; (b) with some prompting, it can identify the one seriously annoying error (which I noticed later in 2015, if memory serves me right), (c) with some more prompting, it can find an ugly fix (to the seriously annoying error) that I saw at the time and that I decided to avoid. I haven't checked the details yet, but the idea of the ugly fix is known to me - in fact it's not much of an idea.

So, yes, an AI-aided formalization effort could take the January 2015 version - or even the 2013 versions - as a basis; let an AI fix the human proof first and proceed from there. I would proceed differently myself.

I have other deadlines, but, if people are genuinely interested, tell me, and I can explain matters in a couple of weeks. There are choices to be made regarding both the final version of the book (I know...) and formalization, and they don't actually concern the above. (The right way to fix things is clear - you do matters in a different way elsewhere, as in the 2019 version, so that the issue doesn't even arise; ChatGPT agrees that that's much better, but then it still has a certain tendency to agree with the user in value judgments.) For instance, I'll probably replace the chapter developing estimates on parabolic cylinder functions by something simpler - there's nothing wrong with it, but at least one referee looks down on special functions, and the saddle-point method would be hard to implement on Lean nowadays, if I understand correctly.

What is a more difficult choice is whether to scuttle a part that is genuinely useful (it saves a factor of log⁡q\sqrt{\log q}logq​ in the minor-arc estimates; of course the main theorem is proved either way, but specialists care about the quality of minor-arc estimates) and is of interest in itself but introduces complications and makes the book a lot longer. It might be best to have 'vanilla' and 'chocolate' versions of the proof here. The 'vanilla' version would be shorter, the 'chocolate' version would rely on a smaller computation as a result of the greater sharpness of its minor-arc bounds.

I take whatever version is formalized now would be conditional on the correctness of computations that have already been done using interval arithmetic. How those computations could be certified nowadays - that's a matter on which I would gladly learn more. Knowing the expense of certifying them would also help in making choices as to how much of a mathematical effort to make so as to reduce them. The ideas are already there, partly written up (see 'vanilla' vs. 'chocolate', and then there are further developments) - it's a matter of sorting things out.

@Harald Helfgott Thank you for the update. Some have suggested to me that path forward would be to create a roadmap for Tao Ceti, but they still aren't accepting finite computations.

IMO, elegant proofs are still worth it. I think finding the simplest or most elegant proof of something is a worthwhile goal in and of itself. I'd imagine AI may lead to greater interest in finding the shortest proofs of things. It just feels elegant.

Do you think the estimation techniques would be applicable to other problems? I think it'd be cool if we could make powerful proof strategies where you could just prove whether f(x) < g(x) for x > n_k or such. Then, the whole proof could simplify to application of a few strategies, perhaps assisted by some sort of CAS-type logic. Could all the techniques applied be put together into a general algorithm that might be applicable to different types of problems? Better yet, could it just take a generating function, and then automatically prove stuff about it? I tried to do more of this when I started, but it took more effort to figure out how to get the AI to use the infrastructure built.

Whether used direct by humans or LLMs, if you have infrastructure to quickly test out ideas, it could probably greatly accelerate their progress.

I've been focused on trying the solve the finite computation challenge. There a number of challenges:
1) Even if theoretically possible to include finite computations in the kernel, it can greatly slow down the build, and make it hard to work with, and build upon. Log tables and such are a nice hack for some things, but applicability is limited.
2) If the computations, don't live in the kernel, then what is sufficiently formalized? Formalization must depend on something. Perhaps, it is a computation model of the CPU, which might depend on a formalization of its architecture, which depends on an understanding of physics and assuming the chip's hardware doesn't contain errors. Some processors may not have fully deterministic computations, and there may not be full formalization or fully formal specs of the processor's behavior. Even if formalizations exist, the CPU manufacturers may not release them.
3) My understanding is that packages like FLINT or libgmp upon which many of the finite computations rest have not been formally verified.
4) So, it has come down to deciding what you are willing accept.
